concept.name: Netting
concept.definition: The offsetting of multiple obligations between parties so that only the net balance must be settled, replacing many gross transfers with a smaller number of net payments or deliveries. Netting may be bilateral (between two parties) or multilateral (across many participants, typically at a central counterparty).
concept.intuition: If I owe you $100 and you owe me $80, we settle $20 one way instead of moving $180 around — scaled up to thousands of trades, this shrinks what actually has to move.
concept.mechanics: A clearinghouse or settlement system aggregates each participant's buys, sells, payments, and receipts per instrument and currency, computes a single net position or obligation per participant, and settles only those net amounts, drastically reducing settlement volume and liquidity needs.
concept.formula: Net obligation of participant i = sum of amounts due to i minus sum of amounts due from i (per instrument/currency); only the residual is settled.
concept.failure_modes: Netting concentrates and redistributes risk into the netting system: its legal enforceability in insolvency is critical (close-out netting rights), and netting reduces gross exposures while leaving the net exposure to the CCP intact.
concept.misconceptions: Netting does not cancel economic exposure or P&L — positions and market risk remain; only the settlement flows are compressed.
concept.example: If a bank's futures desk buys 1,000 contracts and sells 950 of the same contract during the day, the clearinghouse settles margin and variation on the net 50-contract position rather than processing 1,950 gross deliveries.
